The assembly will hear an address by His
Royal Highness, Grand Duke Guom of
Luxembourg. I request protocol to escort
his Royal Highness and invite him to
address the assembly.
Madame President,
excellencies, first and foremost, allow
me to extend my warmest congratulations
to his excellency Dr. Khaled Raman on
his election as president of the General
Assembly.
He can certainly count on Luxembourg's
full support throughout his tenure.
Madame President, the theme that has
been chosen for this general debate can
hardly be more timely.
When I try to paint an honest picture of
the world we live in, one thing strikes
me in particular.
Trust is under growing strain.
trust between nations, trust between
people, and perhaps most importantly,
trust in our ability to work together.
And yet, I believe that trust is
precisely where we should begin.
Not because trust is easy,
but because every lasting achievement of
the international community has begun
with the decision to trust.
This is my first address to this
assembly as head of state of the Grand
Duchy of Luxembourg.
I assumed office less than a year ago.
It is therefore a particular honor to
stand before you today and to reaffirm
from this podium the importance
Luxembourg attaches to the United
Nations and to a rule-based
international order grounded in the rule
of law.
But this moment also makes me reflect on
what the United Nations means from the
perspective of my own generation.
As a relatively young man who has had
the privilege of traveling the world, I
have been fortunate to meet people from
very different cultures, backgrounds,
and traditions.
These experiences have left me with a
simple and lasting conviction.
We can learn a lot from each other.
And I remain convinced that it is only
by working together that we can overcome
the many challenges our world is facing
today.
This conviction is not naive. I am fully
aware of the difficulties confronting
us.
But precisely because the world is
becoming more difficult, I believe we
must resist the temptation to give up on
cooperation.
There has never been a time when
communication between people in
different parts of the world was so
easy. Millions of young people have
virtual friends and acquaintances across
continents through social media, gaming,
and countless other forms of connection.
We have never been so connected, and yet
we seem increasingly unable to trust one
another.
This should make us reflect.
Is it still possible to build a world
order in which respect and the
willingness to work towards common goals
can prevail over the pursuit of
self-interests and power?
I believe it is. But it will require
determination,
dialogue, and a willingness to look
beyond immediate interests. And this is
why the United Nations matters.
Madame President, Luxembourg has
believed in this principle from the very
beginning.
81 years ago, still deeply marked by the
horrors of the Second World War,
Luxembourg was among the 51 founding
members that came together in San
Francisco to lay the foundations of a
new international order.
At the time, we were the smallest
country represented.
We have prospered in the peace that
Europe enjoyed for decades after 1945.
And we have never forgotten that the
peace could not be taken for granted.
It was built generation after generation
by those who chose cooperation over
confrontation.
Today, that peace is being challenged
once again.
Russia's war of aggression against
Ukraine has brought war back to our
continent.
It is a stark reminder that peace
requires constant commitment and that
the principles on which our
international order was built must be
defended.
The United Nations itself was born from
that choice.
Its charter called upon us to unite our
strength to maintain international peace
and security and above all to save
succeeding generations from the scourge
of war.
81 years later that promise is under
considerable pressure
but it has not failed.
Multilateralism
may be imperfect, but disenchantment
should lead us to reform, not to
dismissal.
The question is therefore not whether we
still need multilateralism.
The question is whether we have the
courage to make it better.
Madame la. Madame President,
this brings me to a question that is
very dear to my heart.
What kind of world do we want to
bequeath to future generations? We often
talk about young people as if they came
from the future. Truth be told, they are
already shaping the present.
Therefore, it is incumbent upon us to
ask ourselves if we're really preparing
a future that is going to earn their
trust. My personal experience has done
nothing but reinforce this conviction.
This year, I had the privilege of
succeeding his majesty King Kustaf of
Sweden as honorary chair of the World
Scout Foundation. My long-standing
commitment to the scout movement has
taught me a great deal about the power
of uh intergenerational dialogue,
solidarity, and the values of the scout
movement. It's also taught me something
absolutely fundamental.
Placing our trust in young people means
giving them responsibilities,
allowing them to take action. They're
growing up in a world in which there are
extraordinary possibilities. But it's
also a world where uncertainty runs
deep. Artificial intelligence and other
emerging technologies are already
transforming our way of life and the way
in which we work.
The enthusiasm
they give rise to also goes handinhand
with the very real concerns.
The current debates about the most
extreme risks of AI remind us that
technological progress cannot be
divorced from responsibility.
As we confront these transformations, we
should endow our young people with the
means to develop their critical thinking
skills and their creativity. And this is
exactly what education is supposed to
do. transmit knowledge and competencies,
but also to teach young people to call
things into question to open up to
others and to shoulder your
responsibilities. Against this backdrop,
I believe that we should have one
guiding principle. Human beings should
be at the heart of all of our decision-m
we must protect
the rights, security, and the well-being
of all. We should also listen to young
people, ask them what we can build.
Working hand in hand
through different cultures and
generations. I saw for myself everything
that young people are capable of
accomplishing when we give them our
trust. We give them responsibilities and
the necessary space to take action as
well as when we encourage them to work
together. This is why Luxembourg
supports the UN's youth delegate program
as well as the United Nations youth
office. It is also why our commitment to
education, science, and culture remains
so important in particular through our
term on the executive board of UNESCO
for the period 2025 2029.
It is precisely these qualities which
allow trust to flourish.
Madame President,
Luxembourg's commitment to the United
Nations is underpinned by all three
pillars. Peace and security, human
rights and development.
Solidarity must be translated into
deeds. We continue to allocate 1% of our
national income to
development corporation. We are also
building long-term partnerships with
vulnerable countries.
We remain committed to the multilateral
humanitarian system as well as to all
those who are providing assistance where
it is most needed. The same level of
responsibility applies to peace and
security.
Conflicts affect all human beings,
women, children, older persons, persons
with disabilities, as well as people who
are already vulnerable.
Protecting civilians and defending human
rights
cannot take a backseat to other
considerations.
Luxembourg has unstintingly worked to
contribute to this effort through
peacekeeping operations,
humanitarian interventions,
protecting children affected by armed
conflict, the woman peace and security
agenda as well as uh the mind clearance
humanitarian activities in Ukraine.
The experience we gained as an elected
member of the security council in 2013
and 2014 showed us that elected members
can make a real difference, especially
when the permanent members of the
security council are divided.
It is for this reason that Luxembourg is
asking for member states to place their
trust in it as it seeks a security
council seat for the 2031 2032 period.
We do this humbly
but firm in our conviction.
Our conviction that a small country can
offer up a different perspective, can
bring different positions closer
together and help find common ground.
When this is particularly difficult,
it is the same conviction which guides
our commitment to human rights.
At a time when respect for human rights
is being subjected to growing pressures,
we must resist the temptation to see it
as something that's up for discussion.
Human rights are neither a privilege
reserved for the few nor the expression
of one culture of one political system.
They are the very bedrock of human
dignity.
Our commitment is also concrete.
As a member of the human rights council
for the period 2022 2024,
Luxembourg
took the full measure of just how
important it is to defend human rights
through multilateralism. We continue to
support the office of the high
commissioner for human rights as well as
efforts aimed at uh clarifying the fate
of uh persons who were disappeared in
Syria. Madame President,
restoring trust also means making our
institutions worthy of that trust.
The Security Council must become more
representative, more effective, and more
accountable to the entire membership of
the United Nations.
Africa in particular, and it was said
many times today, should have a stronger
voice.
And when the Security Council is
paralyzed,
the General Assembly must be able to
play its rightful role.
The United Nations must reform so that
it can deliver more effectively,
particularly when resources are
constrained.
But reform must never become an end in
itself. The purpose of institutions is
to serve people.
Ultimately, the test of multilateralism
is not how many resolutions we adopt or
how many meetings we hold.
It's whether a child is safer because of
our decisions. Whether a young P person
can receive an education.
Whether a family can live in dignity,
whether a small country can believe that
international law will protect it when
power alone cannot.
This is why trust matters and this is
why Luxembourg will continue to defend
multilateralism
because we know what happens when it
fails.
Madame President,
climate change reminds us perhaps more
clearly than any other challenge that we
cannot solve global problems by acting
alone.
It transcends borders and generations.
Small island developing states already
experiences consequences that threaten
their very existence.
Luxembourg may be landlocked, but we are
deeply committed to this common effort,
including by drawing on the expertise of
our financial center in green finance.
Our interests may differ, but our future
is shared.
Madame President,
the world is becoming more fragmented.
The international order is under strain.
We need to recognize this reality, but
we should not mistake a world of
competing centers of power for a more
just or stable international order.
For Luxembourg, the answer is clear. Our
experience has taught us that
international law and multilateral
institutions give countries, whatever
their size, a voice and place at the
table.
It is not about resisting a changing
world but to make multilateralism fit
for that world.
I believe this is ultimately what the
United Nations asks of us. Not that we
agree on everything. Not that we abandon
our national interests, but that we
recognize that there are challenges for
which no nation, however powerful, can
find lasting solutions alone.
We can look at the imperfections of
multilateralism and conclude that it no
longer works. or we can reform it
fairly, strengthen it and make it worthy
of the trust that future generations
will place in us.
I know which choice I want to make
because this is the world I want to
leave to my children.
A world where dialogue is stronger than
confrontation. Where respect between
nations allows differences to become
sources of strength rather than
division. Where international law
protects weaks protects the weak as well
as the strong.
If we restore trust, if we listen to the
next generation, and if we have the
courage to act together,
the United Nations can continue to be
more than a reflection of the world as
it is. It can remain an instrument for
building the world we want to leave
behind,
a world worthy of the trust of those who
will inherit it.
Young people do not expect us to solve
every challenge, but they do expect us
to try. They expect us to act with
responsibility.
And above all, they expect us not to
lose faith in our ability to shape a
better future.
And that is the promise we should make
to the next generation. Thank you.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the Grand Duke of Luxembourg.
